item.title: Conflicted Records: Typed Adversarial Contracts for Auditable LLM Output Quality Enforcement
item.description: arXiv:2610.29669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-generated records increasingly populate production information systems where they are treated as data assets subject to the same quality expectations as records from operational databases. A single such record can simultaneously satisfy and violate a quality rule: a grounded fact adjacent to a hallucination, a useful answer adjacent to a stereotype. Classical data cleaning cannot resolve this because the two judgments are incompatible over the same span; a single LLM judge cannot either, since it shares the training biases that produced the conflict. Existing interventions such as prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, and RLHF reduce surface error rates but provide no audit trail and cannot distinguish genuine remediation from blanket suppression. The question is whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch the defects that referential checks alone miss. We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction sharply. The deliberation layer transfers from stereotype to hallucination remediation on HaluEval QA with only role-framing changes, raising right-answer recovery by 49 percentage points; the triage gate required a cross-family second auditor to maintain recall on objective hallucination. Every claim, vote, and instruction is stored as a typed record giving operators a provenance trail auditable under emerging AI regulations.
item.dc:creator: Kardelen Subasi, Jaros{\l}aw A. Chudziak

item.title: WaRP: Workload-Aware Request Planning for Vector Retrieval on Object Storage
item.description: arXiv:2610.29689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern vector search systems keep payload vectors in cloud object storage and only a compact routing index on fast local storage, typically using cluster-based ANN indexes. This design inherits a problem existing systems do not address. On object storage, small Range-GETs have latency dominated by fixed per-request overhead and are billed per request. Existing readers either issue one request per probed cluster, or coalesce adjacent ranges with hand-tuned gap or span thresholds that do not transfer across datasets or query workloads. We formulate the grouping of probed-cluster byte intervals into object-store requests as a global per-query optimization problem and present WaRP, a workload-aware request planner that solves it efficiently. Given the sorted byte intervals, a limit on the number of requests per query, and an estimate of how many object-store requests from one query can proceed concurrently under the target serving configuration, WaRP searches for a merge plan that minimizes a concurrency-aware latency surrogate while satisfying the request limit. Using an optimized dynamic program and adaptive frontier search, WaRP returns a plan within $(1{+}\epsilon)$ of the optimum, with per-query planning overhead under $10$ms even in the most demanding tested settings. A lightweight offline reordering pass further improves request mergeability without changing the semantics of ANN search. We implement WaRP inside Lance's I/O scheduler and evaluate it on AWS S3. We build IVFPQ indexes on seven datasets, including SIFT100M and DEEP100M at the 100M-vector scale. WaRP + Reorder improves QPS by $1.09--3.48\times$ and reduces GETs by $2.12--5.19\times$ relative to Lance, while preserving Lance's recall.
item.dc:creator: Ruipeng Wan, Xinyu Zeng, Yiming Qiao, Huanchen Zhang

item.title: Building SQL Equivalence Proofs from Query Rewrite Rules
item.description: arXiv:2610.30100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Query rewriting and semantic evaluation of text-to-SQL systems both depend on deciding whether two SQL queries return the same result on every database satisfying the schema constraints. Decades of equivalence-preserving optimizer rules provide a natural basis for constructive proofs: two queries are equivalent when admitted rewrites transform them to a common logical expression. Building on this observation, \sys{} organizes query-rewriting knowledge as a standalone proof-producing system. It separates rule validation from proof discovery, explicitly aligns alternative query representations, and returns the resulting rewrite derivation. Across three corpus classes, EquiTrace proves 648/1,106 expected-equivalent text-to-SQL pairs (58.6%), 229/266 curated pairs (86.1%), and 97/240 LLM-generated rewrites whose results agree under benchmark execution (40.4%). On the query rewrite corpus, EquiTrace proves 97 pairs, compared with 35 for QED and 38 for SQLSolver. An analysis of 1,242 recorded proofs shows that coverage depends on a small number of transformations, while many frequently used rules are individually substitutable. The resulting derivations make each proof replayable and expose the specific transformations on which it depends.
item.dc:creator: Chunyu Chen, Xinyi Huang, Zhengjie Miao

item.title: Resilience for Regular Path Queries: Towards a Complexity Classification
item.description: arXiv:2412.09411v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The resilience problem for a query and an input set or bag database is to compute the minimum number of facts to remove from the database to make the query false. In this paper, we study how to compute the resilience of Regular Path Queries (RPQs) over graph databases. Our goal is to characterize the regular languages L for which it is tractable to compute the resilience of the existentially-quantified RPQ built from L. We show that computing the resilience in this sense is tractable (even in combined complexity) for all RPQs defined from so-called local languages. By contrast, we show hardness in data complexity for RPQs defined from the following language classes (after reducing the languages to eliminate redundant words): all finite languages featuring a word containing a repeated letter, and all languages featuring a specific kind of counterexample to being local (which we call four-legged languages). The latter include in particular all languages that are not star-free. Our results also imply a dichotomy on all languages with a so-called neutral letter. We last show tractability for some classes of non-local languages, namely the so-called bipartite chain languages and one-dangling languages, and highlight some remaining obstacles towards a full dichotomy.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Amarilli, Wolfgang Gatterbauer, Neha Makhija, Mika\"el Monet, Mart\'in Mu\~noz

item.title: Efficient Path Query Processing in Relational Database Systems
item.description: arXiv:2604.02553v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Path queries are crucial for property graphs, and there is growing interest in queries that combine regular expressions over labels with constraints on property values of vertices and edges. Efficient evaluation of such general path queries requires that intermediate results be eliminated early when there is no possible completion to a full result path. Neither state-of-the-art (SOA) graph DBMS nor relational DBMS currently can do this effectively for a large class of queries. We show that this problem can be addressed by giving a relational optimizer ``a little help'' by specifying early filtering opportunities explicitly in the query. To this end, we propose ReCAP, an abstraction that greatly simplifies the implementation of early filtering techniques for any type of property constraint for which such early filtering can be derived. No matter how complex the constraint, one only needs to implement (1) an NFA-style state transition function and (2) a handful of functions that mirror those needed for user-defined aggregates. We show that when using ReCAP, a standard relational DBMS like DuckDB can effectively push property constraints deep into the query plan, beating the SOA graph and relational DBMS by a factor up to 400,000 over a variety of queries and input graphs.
item.dc:creator: Diego Rivera Correa, Mirek Riedewald

item.title: Ozone: A Unified Platform for Transportation Research
item.description: arXiv:2604.10959v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transportation research increasingly depends on heterogeneous data from roadside cameras, UAV imagery, LiDAR, and in-vehicle sensors. Differences in data representations, model interfaces, and evaluation protocols complicate cross-dataset benchmarking and reproducibility. We present Ozone, a unified transportation research platform organized around Hardware, Data, Model, and Evaluation layers, with a Prototype layer supporting deployment-oriented applications. Its data layer links vehicle trajectories, traffic conflicts, reconstructed crashes, and digital-twin maps through a shared trajectory schema. The source inventory spans 19 trajectory datasets recorded at 59 sites in eight countries, with completed converters for 12 sources and adaptation ongoing for seven. The converters align coordinate systems, object classes, oriented bounding boxes, and kinematic fields. A shared implementation of surrogate safety measures supports conflict extraction, while map and motion constraints link crash reports to reconstructed trajectories. CARLA digital-twin maps and SUMO traffic logic connect these records to simulation, model development, and evaluation. Validation on 500 vehicles from four datasets reports mean position, heading, and speed errors below 0.15 m, 2.5{\deg}, and 0.3 m/s. A workflow study reports an 85 % reduction in experiment setup time. Case studies demonstrate human-factor experiments and automated-driving safety testing, while the model interfaces support traffic modeling and world-model research. The source code and datasets are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Ou Zheng, Ruyi Feng, Yufeng Yang, Shengxuan Ding, Lishengsa Yue, Ye Li, Baichuan Mo, Yunhan Zheng, Minwei Kong, Dingyi Zhuang, Ao Qu, Zhibin Li, Meng Li, Dongjie Wang, Wangyang Ying

item.title: NousDB - A Fast Query Engine for Semantic Analytics
item.description: arXiv:2610.28551v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Semantic data analytics systems integrate AI-powered operators into query pipelines, enabling declarative queries over structured and unstructured data. However, existing systems rely on per-tuple model invocations, ad hoc operator designs, and lack principled cost models, resulting in poor scalability and limited optimization. We present NousDB, a high-performance semantic analytics engine built on Apache DataFusion[22]. Through NousDB we propose an extended relational algebra with three semantic operators and formal algebraic properties that enable principled query rewriting and cross-operator optimization. We further propose a token-based cost model using equi-depth token histograms to optimize batch sizing under context-window constraints and provide statistical guarantees for safe batching. Experiments show that NousDB achieves up to x86 speedups with both local and enterprise LLMs, while leading competitors in token efficiency and accuracy. These gains extend to complex JOB and Stack workloads augmented with semantic operators, supporting both traditional and semantic analytics.
item.dc:creator: Christos Tsapelas, Georgia Koutrika, Yannis Ioannidis

item.title: VDDP: Verifiable Distributed Differential Privacy under the Client-Server-Verifier Setup
item.description: arXiv:2504.21752v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Although differential privacy (DP) is widely regarded as the de facto standard for data privacy, its implementation remains vulnerable to unfaithful execution by servers, particularly in distributed settings. In such cases, servers may sample noise from incorrect distributions or generate correlated noise while appearing to follow established protocols. This work addresses these malicious behaviours in a distributed client-server-verifier setup under Verifiable Distributed Differential Privacy (VDDP), a novel framework for the verifiable execution of distributed DP mechanisms. We systematically capture end-to-end security and privacy guarantees against potentially colluding adversarial behaviours of clients, servers, and verifiers by characterizing the connections and distinctions between VDDP and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). As our primary instantiation of VDDP, the Verifiable Distributed Discrete Laplace Mechanism (VDDLM) achieves a proving-time speedup ranging from 50x to 4,000,000x over existing solutions, with larger gains in stronger-privacy regimes. Furthermore, the VDDLM sampling circuit achieves asymptotically lower overhead than prior constructions and is applicable to a broad range of cryptography-based DP applications.
item.dc:creator: Haochen Sun, Xi He

item.title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.20208v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Can We Trust AI Evaluation? Robustness, Causality, and Risk in Modern AI Assessment Workshop - NeurIPS 2026, Sydney, Australia, Dec 2026, Sydney (Australia), Australia

item.title: Latent Bridges for Multi-Table Question Answering
item.description: arXiv:2606.28916v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce GRAB, a constructor-encoder-bridge pipeline for table question answering. Our method lifts relational data into an heterogeneous graph, encodes it via message passing, and transfers the signals to an LLM through a small set of query-conditioned latent tokens. This provides the LLM with a compact, task-relevant structural representation together with the flattened text. Crucially, the LLM remains strictly frozen to preserve its general reasoning capabilities; we train only the lightweight graph encoder and latent bridge (91M parameters), allowing the entire pipeline to be trained efficiently. Our pipeline significantly improves performance on relational Question Answering, with the largest gains in demanding multi-table settings, offering an efficient, principled way to connect relational deep learning with LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Simone Varriale, Tamara Cucumides, Floris Geerts, Paolo Papotti
